name: Third-Party Risk
tagline: Your security is the minimum of yours and your suppliers’.

org.name: Northgate Logistics
org.brief: A 1,800-person logistics company that outsources heavily: a managed service provider runs its endpoints and servers with domain-wide admin rights, a payroll SaaS and an ERP vendor feed the finance platform, customs lodgement runs through the ERP vendor’s integration, and a software vendor’s desktop client auto-updates on every warehouse PC. Contracts were signed by procurement; nobody has tested the exit clause.

regimes.name: APRA CPS 230 (if you are a regulated customer) and customer contracts
regimes.note: Regulated customers must manage material service providers and their sub-contractors, and will push the same obligations to you through contracts.

regimes.name: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) — Notifiable Data Breaches
regimes.note: You remain accountable for personal information your suppliers hold on your behalf. A supplier breach can be your eligible data breach.

regimes.name: NIST SP 800-161 & ASD supply chain guidance
regimes.note: Good-practice frameworks for cyber supply chain risk management: assess, contract, monitor and plan the exit.

assets.name: Corporate Email
assets.desc: Staff email, including booking and customs correspondence.

assets.name: Offices & Warehouse PCs
assets.desc: Managed endpoints that run the software vendor’s auto-updating client.

assets.name: MSP Remote Management
assets.desc: The managed service provider’s RMM and privileged-access tooling with admin rights across the estate.

assets.name: Software Vendor Update Channel
assets.desc: The vendor’s update service and signing infrastructure that Northgate trusts implicitly.

assets.name: Directory & SSO
assets.desc: Active Directory and SSO, with MSP accounts in Domain Admins.

assets.name: ERP & Transport Management
assets.desc: Bookings, billing and the vendor-maintained integrations to finance and customs.

assets.name: Finance & Payroll
assets.desc: Payment runs, supplier bank details and payroll.

assets.name: Customer & Shipment Data
assets.desc: Customer contracts, consignment details and customs records.

assets.name: Backups (MSP-managed)
assets.desc: Backups run and held by the MSP under the same admin credentials.

systems.name: Managed service provider access
systems.blurb: The MSP’s engineers administer Northgate’s estate through a privileged-access gateway and an RMM platform whose agents run on every server and PC. Shared admin credentials are checked out of a vault.

scenarios.text: An MSP engineer’s credentials are phished at a conference, and the attacker signs in to the gateway as that engineer.
scenarios.why: The attacker is accepted as a trusted supplier employee. Nothing has been changed yet; the failure is identity assurance for a third party.

scenarios.text: An attacker who controls the RMM platform pushes a malicious script through the normal agent channel to every managed server at once.
scenarios.why: Legitimate-looking commands are altered or injected on the way to the fleet. Integrity of the flow failed; the channel itself worked as designed.

scenarios.text: The shared credential vault is readable by every MSP staff member and holds the admin passwords of all the MSP’s customers.
scenarios.why: Sensitive credentials are readable by people who should not hold them, across customer boundaries. Nothing is altered or taken down.

scenarios.text: A junior MSP help-desk role can create new domain administrator accounts for any customer through the gateway.
scenarios.why: A role holds authority beyond what it needs. The failure is excessive privilege design, not impersonation or interception.

scenarios.text: An intruder edits the asset database to mark compromised servers as decommissioned, so they drop out of patching and monitoring.
scenarios.why: Stored data that later decisions rely on is changed without authority. This is tampering with the store.

scenarios.text: Repeated failed administrative logins from a compromised supplier tool trigger account lockouts on hundreds of servers during month-end processing.
scenarios.why: The channel becomes unusable for legitimate administrators through lockout storms. Nothing is forged, altered or read.

scenarios.text: RMM scripts run as a shared service account and logs do not record which engineer launched them, so a destructive script cannot be attributed.
scenarios.why: There is no attributable record of who performed an action. That is the defining Repudiation problem.

scenarios.text: The MSP records remote sessions with a third-party screen-capture tool that stores screenshots, including Northgate customer data, in another country.
scenarios.why: The contents of the flow end up with a party and in a place nobody agreed to. Nothing is changed or blocked.

systems.name: Software vendors & SaaS integrations
systems.blurb: A vendor’s desktop client auto-updates from the vendor’s service and talks to the ERP. A payroll SaaS posts webhooks through an integration API into the ERP, which posts to finance.

scenarios.text: An attacker steals the vendor’s code-signing credentials and publishes an update that every customer’s client installs as genuine.
scenarios.why: The attacker is accepted as the vendor. Nothing in Northgate has been changed yet; trust in the supplier’s identity is what failed.

scenarios.text: The client downloads updates over plain HTTP and does not verify a signature, so a network attacker swaps the package for a malicious one.
scenarios.why: The content of the update is altered in transit and executed. Integrity of the flow failed, not secrecy or availability.

scenarios.text: Integration API keys sit in a plaintext configuration file readable by every IT contractor and by the vendor’s support staff.
scenarios.why: Sensitive stored secrets are readable by people who should not hold them. Nothing is altered; the failure is confidentiality.

scenarios.text: The vendor client’s background service runs as SYSTEM and accepts commands from any local user, which a warehouse employee uses to gain administrator rights.
scenarios.why: A low-privileged user gains authority it was never granted. The employee is not impersonating anyone; the privilege boundary failed.

scenarios.text: An attacker with access to the finance data changes a supplier’s bank account details, and the next payment run pays the attacker.
scenarios.why: Stored data that drives payments is changed without authority. This is tampering with the store, the core of business email compromise outcomes.

scenarios.text: A flood of webhooks, whether an attack or a vendor bug, overwhelms the integration API and payroll cannot be processed before pay day.
scenarios.why: The channel is overwhelmed and unavailable to legitimate use at a critical time. Nothing is forged, altered or read.

scenarios.text: All vendor integrations use one service account, so when a batch of fraudulent postings appears nobody can tell which integration or person created them.
scenarios.why: There is no attributable evidence of which actor performed the action. That is the defining Repudiation problem.

scenarios.text: API keys are sent in URL query strings that appear in web proxy and CDN logs readable by several teams and a logging vendor.
scenarios.why: The contents of the flow are exposed in places that should never have them. Nothing is altered and the integration still works.

ttx.name: Cloud Hopper at Northgate
ttx.blurb: Your managed service provider is compromised and its trusted access becomes the intruder’s. Modelled on the documented menuPass/APT10 campaigns against MSPs (MITRE G0045). Decide how much trust to cut, what your contract actually gives you, and what you must tell customers.

injects.title: A 03:00 admin session from the MSP
injects.text: The SIEM flags a domain-admin session from the MSP’s gateway at 03:00 Sunday. No change ticket exists and the engineer named on the account is on leave.

decision.prompt: What does the on-call analyst do?

choices.label: Treat it as compromise of the supplier account: suspend that account and the MSP’s standing domain-admin access, preserve logs, and call the MSP’s named incident contact on the contractual emergency number.
choices.lesson: A trusted account behaving out of pattern is an intrusion until proven otherwise. Act on the identity, not on the supplier relationship, and use the contract’s emergency channel.

choices.label: Email the MSP service desk and ask whether it was them.
choices.lesson: Asking by email through the same potentially compromised channel wastes the hours that matter.

choices.label: Assume it is a roster mix-up and check on Monday.
choices.lesson: Weekend, off-hours supplier access is exactly the window these actors use.

injects.title: The MSP says it is “looking into it”
injects.text: The MSP acknowledges the alert but says it cannot share logs until its own investigation is complete, and asks Northgate not to take any action that might “disrupt service”.

choices.label: Invoke the incident and audit clauses in the contract, demand logs and a named responder within hours, and in parallel cut the MSP’s access paths and rotate any credential it held, running critical processes manually.
choices.lesson: Your obligations to your customers do not wait on your supplier’s investigation. Use the contract, and protect yourself technically in parallel.

choices.label: Wait for the MSP’s report.
choices.lesson: Waiting hands the initiative to the intruder and to a supplier with its own interests.

choices.label: Give the MSP more access so it can investigate faster.
choices.lesson: Handing more privilege to a possibly-compromised supplier is the intruder’s best case.

injects.title: The freight stops
injects.text: Cutting the MSP’s access has stopped automated patching and the nightly backup. The warehouse management system’s remote support is also offline, and trucks are queuing.

decision.prompt: How do you balance containment and operations?

choices.label: Run critical flows on documented manual procedures, restore only the minimum supplier paths through a monitored, time-boxed bastion that Northgate controls, and communicate expected delays to customers.
choices.lesson: You can rarely cut a supplier completely. Re-admit them through a path you control, scoped and watched, and tell customers early.

choices.label: Restore the MSP’s original access to get freight moving.
choices.lesson: Restoring the same access restores the attacker’s access too.

choices.label: Do nothing and let the queue build.
choices.lesson: Inaction trades one harm for another with no containment benefit.

injects.title: Customer notification clocks
injects.text: Two large customers’ contracts require notice within 24 hours of a security incident that may affect their data. Forensics has not yet confirmed whether shipment data was accessed.

choices.label: Notify both customers now with what is known, what is not, containment steps and next update time; begin the NDB assessment in parallel; ask counsel to review.
choices.lesson: Contract clocks run from awareness. A candid early notice with caveats beats a perfect late one.

choices.label: Say nothing until forensics confirms access.
choices.lesson: Missing a contractual clock is a second incident layered on the first.

choices.label: Send a vague “maintenance” notice.
choices.lesson: A misleading notice is worse than a late one when the truth emerges.

injects.title: Do we stay with this MSP?
injects.text: The board asks whether to terminate the MSP, switch providers, or insource, and what the exit would cost.

choices.label: Decide on evidence after the review, but start now: separate admin tiers and credentials per customer, own your backups and break-glass accounts, test an exit plan and consider a second provider for critical services.
choices.lesson: Concentration risk is reduced by independence (your own backups and break-glass), segmentation of supplier privilege and a tested exit, whatever you decide about the supplier.

choices.label: Terminate immediately and rebuild in-house.
choices.lesson: A rushed exit without capability transfers the risk rather than removing it.

choices.label: Renew with a discount and a stronger SLA.
choices.lesson: An SLA does not fix privilege design or the absence of an exit plan.

objectives.text: Keep finance and customer data safe

govern.spoofing.name: Supplier Access Policy
govern.spoofing.flavour: Supplier staff are staff, only less known
govern.spoofing.desc: Policy that treats supplier access like employee access: named accounts, MFA, approved windows, least privilege, joiner-mover-leaver, and recorded privileged sessions.

govern.tampering.name: Third-party Assurance Programme
govern.tampering.desc: Tiered supplier assessments driven by criticality: evidence-based reviews for the few that matter, contract security schedules, audit rights and incident-notification clocks.

identify.tampering.name: Supplier & Dependency Register
identify.tampering.flavour: Who touches what, and who do they use?
identify.tampering.desc: An inventory of suppliers, what each can access, which systems depend on them and their key sub-contractors (fourth parties), updated when contracts change.

identify.disclosure.name: Supplier Data Flow Map
identify.disclosure.flavour: Which supplier holds your customers’ data?
identify.disclosure.desc: A map of what personal and sensitive data each supplier receives, where it is stored and processed, and how it returns or is destroyed on exit.

protect.spoofing.name: Just-in-time Supplier Access
protect.spoofing.flavour: No standing admin for people you do not employ
protect.spoofing.desc: Supplier accounts have no standing privilege: access is requested, approved, time-boxed and recorded, with phishing-resistant MFA.

protect.tampering.name: Update Verification & Staging
protect.tampering.flavour: Trust the signature, not the sender
protect.tampering.desc: Vendor updates are verified (signature, hash, provenance), staged on a pilot ring and monitored before broad rollout, so a poisoned release does not reach every endpoint at once.

protect.elevation.name: Tiered Admin & MSP Boundaries
protect.elevation.flavour: The MSP admins their world, not yours
protect.elevation.desc: Separate admin tiers and accounts per customer, no shared credentials across the MSP’s customers, and break-glass accounts that Northgate controls.

detect.tampering.name: Supplier Activity Monitoring
detect.tampering.desc: Monitoring tuned to supplier behaviour: admin logins out of window, bulk commands from RMM tools, new accounts and remote tools appearing, with a baseline of normal MSP activity.

respond.elevation.name: Supplier Containment Playbook
respond.elevation.flavour: Cut the supplier, keep the freight moving
respond.elevation.desc: A rehearsed procedure to suspend a supplier’s access, rotate shared secrets, run key processes manually and bring up an alternative, with decision rights agreed in advance.

respond.disclosure.name: Joint Incident & Notification Runbook
respond.disclosure.flavour: Who calls whom, in which hour
respond.disclosure.desc: Contractual and practical incident-notification terms with suppliers (hours, not days), and a joint runbook for assessing and notifying customers, regulators and the OAIC.

recover.dos.name: Exit & Substitution Plan
recover.dos.flavour: A tested exit clause is a control
recover.dos.desc: Backups held independently of the supplier, documented data export, and a tested plan to move a critical service in-house or to a second supplier.

cards.name: Just-in-time Vendor Sessions
cards.desc: Supplier access is requested, approved, time-boxed and recorded. Counters Trusted Relationship abuse.
cards.lesson: Standing admin for a supplier is a standing target. When access exists only for an approved hour, a stolen credential is worth almost nothing the rest of the time.

cards.name: Staged Update Rings
cards.desc: Vendor updates reach a small pilot ring first and are watched before wider rollout. Counters poisoned releases.
cards.lesson: The 3CX and SolarWinds payloads reached customers as normal signed updates. A pilot ring turns “everyone at once” into “ten machines and an alert”.

cards.name: Invoke Contractual Incident Support
cards.desc: Use the supplier’s contractual incident obligations: reveal up to 3 footholds (stealth ≤ 5), restore 2 Resilience, draw 1. Spent for the rest of the run.
cards.lesson: A contract is only a control if it gives you something at 3 a.m.: logs within hours, named incident contacts, audit rights and the supplier’s engineers on your bridge.

cards.name: Vendor Software Verification
cards.desc: Check a vendor release against hashes and provenance: reveal a foothold (stealth ≤ 4), block spread into the asset this round, +1 intel.
cards.lesson: Verifying what the vendor actually shipped against a second source is cheap, and it is the step that caught several supply chain compromises before widespread impact.

relics.name: Tested Exit Plan
relics.lesson: A supplier you can leave is a supplier you can negotiate with, and one whose failure is survivable.
